clue.text: The objectivity of a task force

definitions.meaning: impartiality, standing apart from a matter emotionally
a body of troops sent off on a separate mission

explanation.surface: Someone praises the impartial outlook of a military task force.
explanation.definitionFit: Both senses come from being separated: aloofness of mind, and a unit separated from the main army for a special job.

clue.text: It is liable to slip in a bad skid

indicators.note: bad suggests the letters of skid are in poor order and need rearranging

explanation.surface: A warning that something may slide away when a car goes into a nasty skid.
explanation.walkthrough: 'bad' rearranges SKID. The definition alludes to a slipped disc in the spine, spelt the American way here.
explanation.definitionFit: A spinal cartilage pad can slip out of place, the injury called a slipped disc.

clue.text: Linen has the correct marking

definitions.meaning: strong linen or cotton cloth used for mattress covers
putting a check mark beside something to show it is right

explanation.surface: A sheet of linen bears the proper laundry label.
explanation.definitionFit: The fabric is the striped cloth used for mattress covers; the other sense is the act of putting check marks against right answers.

clue.text: Talk of soldiers upset about score? On the contrary

indicators.note: about means one piece goes round the other
on the contrary reverses the stated arrangement, so the score goes around the soldiers instead

parts.note: in rugby a conversion is a kick at goal that scores extra points

indicators.note: upset in a down clue means the word for soldiers is turned upside down, read backwards

parts.note: TA is the Territorial Army, Britain's reserve soldiers

explanation.surface: A chat among troops who are annoyed about a match result, or perhaps the reverse.
explanation.walkthrough: Read literally, upset soldiers go round the score; 'On the contrary' flips which piece holds which. A rugby conversion scores two points after a try.
explanation.definitionFit: A conversation is a spoken exchange, a chat between people.

clue.text: Girl I spoil at first with money

indicators.note: at first tells us the word for spoil comes before I rather than after

parts.note: to mar something is to spoil it
gold stands for money or wealth

explanation.surface: A young woman admits she spoiled things at the start by bringing cash.
explanation.walkthrough: The clue lists I before spoil, but 'at first' moves MAR to the front.
explanation.definitionFit: Marigold is a female first name, taken from the flower.

clue.text: Unadorned, it's set up in part of the church

indicators.note: in puts the turned piece inside the church part

parts.note: the nave is the main body of a church

indicators.note: set up in a down clue means the word is raised, read from bottom to top

parts.note: it, with the 's as is acting as a link

explanation.surface: Something plain is installed in a section of a church.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Unadorned' looks like a describing word for the church but is the definition; native gold, for instance, is gold found plain and pure.
explanation.definitionFit: Native can mean in a natural, plain state, as with metal found pure without refining.

clue.text: Turn in silver expectantly

indicators.note: in places the word for turn within the silver symbol

parts.note: Ag is the chemical symbol for silver
a go is a turn in a game

explanation.surface: A player waits eagerly for their go with the silver.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means eagerly waiting, all excited for what comes next.

clue.text: Birds include a small number of Italian natives

indicators.note: include means the birds contain the abbreviation

parts.note: geese are large water birds
no is the short form of number

explanation.surface: Some birds hold a handful of Italian locals among them.
explanation.definitionFit: People from Genoa, the port city in north-west Italy, are called Genoese.

clue.text: A harmless glider, except when the second part is in the first

definitions.text: A harmless glider, except when the second part is in the first

parts.words: A harmless glider, except when the second part is in the first
parts.note: a non-venomous serpent; put the second word inside the first, as in the phrase snake in the grass, and it becomes a hidden traitor

explanation.surface: Something gliding is safe unless its parts are rearranged.
explanation.walkthrough: 'glider' suggests an aircraft but means a slithering creature. A snake in the grass is a proverbial treacherous person.
explanation.definitionFit: This common European reptile is non-venomous and lives in grassland, so it is a harmless gliding creature.

clue.text: Inferior 24 holding prisoner, curse it!

indicators.note: holding means the first word goes around the others

parts.note: 24 across means perceive or spot, the same as see
con is short for convict, a prisoner
drat is a mild curse, as in drat it!

explanation.surface: Someone shouts in frustration about a poor-quality prisoner.
explanation.walkthrough: The cross-reference 24 points to 24 across, whose definition is perceive, so a synonym of that answer is needed, not its letters.
explanation.definitionFit: Second-rate means of poor quality, below the best standard.

clue.text: She finds a new element in common salt

parts.note: Na is sodium, which with chlorine makes common salt

explanation.surface: A woman discovers a fresh chemical in table salt.
explanation.definitionFit: Anna is a woman's given name, so it is a female person.

clue.text: Sort of prayer best in a Calvinist

indicators.note: sort as a verb means arrange, so these letters are put in a new order

explanation.surface: A Calvinist kind of prayer is said to be the finest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sort of' rearranges PRAYER BEST IN; the 'a' is a link.
explanation.definitionFit: Presbyterian churches follow the Reformed theology of John Calvin.

clue.text: Season the first of the fish

indicators.note: first of picks out the opening letter of the following word

parts.note: the ide is a European freshwater fish

explanation.surface: Spring arrives with the first catch of fish.
explanation.walkthrough: The opening 'the' is a link; the second 'the' gives T.
explanation.definitionFit: Tide is an old word for a time of year, as in Yuletide or Eastertide.

clue.text: Teacher's journey with writer by ship

parts.note: to go is to journey
Jules Verne, the French novelist
SS stands for steamship

explanation.surface: A tutor takes a trip with an author on a boat.
explanation.walkthrough: The 's in Teacher's is short for is, linking definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: A governess is a woman employed to educate children in a private household.

clue.text: It's too big to give us our deserts, do we hear?

definitions.text: It's too big to give us our deserts, do we hear?

parts.words: It's too big to give us our deserts, do we hear?
parts.note: deserts said aloud is desserts; a large serving spoon is bigger than the one meant for puddings

explanation.surface: Something is too great to hand out what we deserve.
explanation.walkthrough: Getting one's deserts means getting what one deserves, but 'do we hear' points to desserts: the spoon is larger than a dessertspoon.
explanation.definitionFit: This serving spoon holds more than the smaller spoon used for eating puddings.

clue.text: When winter returns, said Byron, lazy outsiders appear with dignity

parts.note: Byron joked that the English winter ends in July and starts again in August

indicators.note: outsiders picks the first and last letters of lazy

explanation.surface: A poet remarks on winter's comeback while idlers look stately.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron's Don Juan quip calls the English winter 'ending in July, to recommence in August'. LY is the first and last letters of 'lazy'.
explanation.definitionFit: Doing something in an august way means with majesty and grandeur.

clue.text: Part of Foot Prussian leader left behind

indicators.note: left means that letter has gone away from the word

parts.note: the pastern is part of a horse's foot, between fetlock and hoof

indicators.note: leader means the first letter of Prussian

explanation.surface: A piece of a foot is abandoned when a Prussian commander leaves.
explanation.walkthrough: Foot is capitalised to suggest a person or regiment, but it is a horse's foot. Removing P gives the nautical word for at the back.
explanation.definitionFit: On a ship, astern means at or towards the rear.

clue.text: A shipbuilder's line in footwear

definitions.meaning: the load line marked on a hull
a light canvas sports shoe with a rubber sole

explanation.surface: A ship maker's range of shoes.
explanation.walkthrough: In Britain a plimsoll is a canvas gym shoe, a sneaker.
explanation.definitionFit: The load mark on a hull bears Samuel Plimsoll's name, and the canvas shoe shares it because its rubber band resembles that mark.

clue.text: Windows displaying cat food

definitions.meaning: panes that let daylight into a room
animal lungs, once sold as pet meat

explanation.surface: A shop window shows off tins of pet food.
explanation.walkthrough: Lights are the lungs of slaughtered animals, traditionally fed to cats.
explanation.definitionFit: Windows are openings that admit daylight; offal lungs, butchers' meat for pets, share the name.

clue.text: Pigment from spongy ground in quarry

indicators.note: in places the marsh word inside the prey word

parts.note: quarry is hunted prey, which is game
a bog is wet, spongy ground

explanation.surface: A colouring is extracted from boggy land in a pit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'quarry' suggests a stone pit; here it means hunted animals.
explanation.definitionFit: Gamboge is a yellow gum resin used by artists as a colouring.

clue.text: Quietly give a new, slant to sound reproduction?

parts.note: p, piano, is the musical direction for quietly
to lay back is to tilt something backwards to a new angle

explanation.surface: Softly offering a fresh angle on audio recording.
explanation.definitionFit: Playback is the replaying of recorded audio.

clue.text: Stop a creeper overrunning the pitch

indicators.note: overrunning in a down clue puts the snake above the word for stop

parts.note: the asp is a snake, a creature that creeps
to halt is to stop

explanation.surface: A climbing plant halts its spread over a sports field.
explanation.walkthrough: 'creeper' suggests ivy and 'pitch' a sports ground; the creeper is a snake and pitch is tar.
explanation.definitionFit: Asphalt is a black bituminous material like tar, used to surface roads.

clue.text: One engaged as cook in cafe

indicators.note: to cook the books is to fiddle them, so these letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone takes a job as a chef in a café.
explanation.walkthrough: 'One engaged' sounds like a hired worker but means someone betrothed; 'cook' rearranges IN CAFE.
explanation.definitionFit: A fiancé is a man who has promised to marry.

clue.text: Discussion group having a drinking party

definitions.meaning: a conference or meeting where experts debate a subject
in ancient Greece, a convivial gathering for wine and talk

explanation.surface: A committee meeting turns into a booze-up.
explanation.walkthrough: The OCR read 'a' as '2'; the page prints 'having a'.
explanation.definitionFit: Today the word means an academic conference; in classical Athens it was an evening of wine and debate, as in Plato's dialogue.

clue.text: Some of those mysteries Pythagoras helps us to perceive

indicators.note: some of means only part of the following words is used, a run of letters inside them

explanation.surface: Greek geometry helps us understand certain mysteries.
explanation.walkthrough: The letters run across the end of 'mysteries' and the start of 'Pythagoras'.
explanation.definitionFit: To espy is to catch sight of, to spot.

clue.text: Soldiers guarding a base?

indicators.note: guarding tells us the soldiers surround the next piece like sentries

parts.note: men are ordinary soldiers, as in officers and men

explanation.surface: Troops are standing watch over a military camp.
explanation.walkthrough: 'base' looks like a military camp but is the adjective meaning low or ignoble.
explanation.definitionFit: Mean and base both describe someone contemptible or ignoble.

clue.text: Bespectacled bishop takes a pound for old coin

parts.note: B for bishop with a pair of O shapes, like spectacle lenses, around it
L, from Latin libra, is the symbol for a pound

explanation.surface: A churchman in glasses accepts a pound for an antique coin.
explanation.walkthrough: Spectacles are OO in crosswords, two round lenses; B for bishop wears them.
explanation.definitionFit: The obol was a small silver coin of ancient Greece.

clue.text: Excite trendy member holding team pet

parts.note: in means fashionable

indicators.note: holding means the body part goes around the team and pet

parts.note: a toe is a member, part of the body
XI, eleven, is a cricket or football team
a cat is a household pet

explanation.surface: A fashionable player with the club mascot stirs everyone up.
explanation.walkthrough: 'member' suggests a club member but means a limb or digit.
explanation.definitionFit: To intoxicate can mean to exhilarate or make wildly excited, beyond its sense of making drunk.

clue.text: Possibly Father Christmas?

parts.note: the French name for Santa is Père Noël, and the second word is also a man's name who might be a father

explanation.surface: Is this perhaps Santa Claus?
explanation.walkthrough: The French call Father Christmas Père Noël, so the word can mean Christmas itself or a man so named who may be a dad.
explanation.definitionFit: The word is a carol or the Christmas season, and Father Christmas is Père Noël in France.

clue.text: Duke, before and after decapitation

parts.note: the victor of Waterloo was a duke; remove his head letter and you have the jazz bandleader Duke Ellington

explanation.surface: A nobleman, both before and after being beheaded.
explanation.walkthrough: Duke Ellington was a famous jazz composer and bandleader; the Iron Duke defeated Napoleon at Waterloo.
explanation.definitionFit: Arthur Wellesley, victor of Waterloo, held the ducal title; lose the first letter and you have Duke Ellington.
